questions.title: Division vs Truncation
questions.objective: Demonstrate the differences between float division (/), floor division (//), and truncation toward zero int(a / b) on positive and negative inputs.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: In computer arithmetic, dividing integers can produce different outcomes depending on the division model applied:
1. Float Division (`/`): Performs standard floating-point division.
2. Floor Division (`//`): Rounds down to the nearest mathematical integer towards negative infinity (standard Python behavior).
3. Truncation toward Zero (`int(a / b)`): Discards the fractional part, rounding towards zero.

Given two space-separated integers A and B (where B != 0), compute and print the three values in the exact format shown below. Float division must be formatted to exactly 4 decimal places.
questions.input_format: A single line containing two space-separated integers A and B.
questions.output_format:
Three lines:
Line 1: Float: <float_result:.4f>
Line 2: Floor: <floor_result>
Line 3: Trunc: <trunc_result>
hints: Standard float division in Python uses the single slash / operator.
Floor division in Python (//) rounds down towards negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4.
To truncate toward zero for negative numbers, cast the float division result to an integer using int().
questions.reference_solution:
a, b = map(int, input().split())
f_div = a / b
fl_div = a // b
tr_div = int(a / b)
print(f"Float: {f_div:.4f}")
print(f"Floor: {fl_div}")
print(f"Trunc: {tr_div}")

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing two space-separated integers A and B.
extra_fields.output_format:
Three lines:
Line 1: Float: <float_result:.4f>
Line 2: Floor: <floor_result>
Line 3: Trunc: <trunc_result>

Line 2: Kelvin: <K:.2f>

Add 273.15 directly to Celsius for Kelvin.
Format with :.2f in an f-string to guarantee exactly two digits after the decimal point.
questions.reference_solution:
c = float(input())
f = c * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0
k = c + 273.15
print(f"Fahrenheit: {f:.2f}")
print(f"Kelvin: {k:.2f}")

questions.title: Type Inspection & Validation
questions.objective: Classify incoming string tokens as INTEGER, FLOAT, or STRING representations without relying on exception handling.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Write a classifier that inspects a single string token and determines what fundamental numeric or textual type it represents:
- Print "INTEGER" if the token represents a valid integer (optional leading '+' or '-' followed strictly by one or more digits).
- Print "FLOAT" if the token represents a valid float containing exactly one decimal point (with an optional leading sign, and at least one digit in the string).
- Print "STRING" for all other tokens (alphanumeric text, words, symbols, or multiple decimal points).
questions.input_format: A single line containing a single token without surrounding whitespace.
questions.output_format: Print exactly one of: INTEGER, FLOAT, or STRING.
questions.constraints: 1 <= len(token) <= 50; the token contains only printable ASCII characters and no spaces.
hints: Check if stripping an optional leading '+' or '-' leaves only digits using .isdigit().
If the token contains exactly one '.', split around it; the token is a FLOAT when each side is empty or all digits (after an optional sign on the left), and at least one digit exists overall.
If it fits neither numeric definition, classify it as STRING.
questions.reference_solution:
s = input().strip()
sign_len = 1 if s.startswith(('-', '+')) else 0
body = s[sign_len:]
if body and body.isdigit():
    print("INTEGER")
elif '.' in s and len(s.split('.')) == 2:
    parts = s.split('.')
    left, right = parts
    left_valid = (left[1:].isdigit() if left.startswith(('-', '+')) else left.isdigit()) or (left in ('', '-', '+'))
    right_valid = right.isdigit() or right == ''
    total_digits = sum(c.isdigit() for c in s)
    if left_valid and right_valid and total_digits > 0:
        print("FLOAT")
    else:
        print("STRING")
else:
    print("STRING")

extra_fields.time_complexity: O(N) where N is token length
extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing a single token without surrounding whitespace.
extra_fields.output_format: Print exactly one of: INTEGER, FLOAT, or STRING.

questions.title: Rounding vs Truncation
questions.objective: Contrast round(v, 2), f-string :.2f rounding, and arithmetic truncation int(v * 100) / 100, and observe float-representation effects.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Different precision policies can give different results on boundary values:
1. Built-in rounding (`round(v, 2)`): rounds the stored binary float value to 2 decimals. Output formatted to 4 decimals.
2. Formatted String (`f"{v:.2f}"`): rounds the same stored value to 2 decimals for display. It normally agrees with `round()`; it only differs in type (str vs float).
3. Truncation toward Zero (`int(v * 100) / 100`): discards digits beyond 2 decimals without rounding. Because v * 100 is computed in binary floating point, some values (e.g. 1.15 or 0.29) truncate one cent lower than expected. Output formatted to 2 decimals.

Given a float V, compute and print the three values in the exact format shown below.
questions.input_format: A single line containing a float V.
questions.output_format:
Three lines:
Line 1: Round: <round_val:.4f>
Line 2: Format: <format_val>
Line 3: Trunc: <trunc_val:.2f>
hints: Pass 2 as the second argument to round(v, 2), then print with :.4f.
Use f'{v:.2f}' directly for the second line.
Multiply by 100, convert to int, and divide back by 100.0 for truncation toward zero.
questions.reference_solution:
v = float(input())
r_val = round(v, 2)
fmt_val = f"{v:.2f}"
trunc_val = int(v * 100.0) / 100.0
print(f"Round: {r_val:.4f}")
print(f"Format: {fmt_val}")
print(f"Trunc: {trunc_val:.2f}")

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing a float V.
extra_fields.output_format:
Three lines:
Line 1: Round: <round_val:.4f>
Line 2: Format: <format_val>
Line 3: Trunc: <trunc_val:.2f>

questions.title: Systematic SIP Value
questions.objective: Compute future value of recurring monthly SIP investments using annuity compounding formula.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Compute the maturity value of a monthly Systematic Investment Plan (SIP).
Given:
- Monthly investment P (float)
- Expected annual return rate R in percentage (float)
- Investment tenure Y in whole years (integer value, e.g. 5 or 5.0)

Formulas:
- Total months: n = int(Y * 12)
- Monthly periodic rate: i = (R / 100) / 12
- If R == 0: Maturity = P * n
- If R > 0: Maturity = P * [((1 + i)^n - 1) / i] * (1 + i)
- Total Invested = P * n
- Wealth Gained = Maturity - Total Invested

Output all three values formatted to two decimal places.
questions.input_format: A single line containing three space-separated numbers: P R Y.
questions.output_format:
Three lines:
Line 1: Invested: <inv:.2f>
Line 2: Maturity: <mat:.2f>
Line 3: Wealth Gained: <gain:.2f>
hints: Total months n = int(Y * 12). Total invested is P * n.
The monthly rate is i = (R / 100) / 12.
Use the annuity-due formula: multiply P * ((1 + i)**n - 1) / i by (1 + i) at the end. If R == 0 there is no growth, so maturity equals total invested.
questions.reference_solution:
p, r, y = map(float, input().split())
n = int(y * 12)
invested = p * n
if r == 0:
    fv = invested
else:
    i = (r / 100.0) / 12.0
    fv = p * (((1.0 + i)**n - 1.0) / i) * (1.0 + i)
gain = fv - invested
print(f"Invested: {invested:.2f}")
print(f"Maturity: {fv:.2f}")
print(f"Wealth Gained: {gain:.2f}")

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing three space-separated numbers: P R Y.
extra_fields.output_format:
Three lines:
Line 1: Invested: <inv:.2f>
Line 2: Maturity: <mat:.2f>
Line 3: Wealth Gained: <gain:.2f>

questions.title: Date String Parsing & Reassembly
questions.objective: Parse fixed DD-MM-YYYY string slices and reassemble into YYYY/MM/DD and DD.MM.YY.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Parse a date string in fixed-width DD-MM-YYYY format using string slicing (not split, not the datetime module) and reassemble it into two formats:
1. ISO Slash Format: YYYY/MM/DD
2. Dot Short-Year Format: DD.MM.YY (YY is the last two digits of the year)

All inputs are valid calendar dates. Keep leading zeros exactly as given.
questions.input_format: A single line containing a date string in DD-MM-YYYY format.
questions.output_format:
Two lines:
Line 1: Format 1: <YYYY/MM/DD>
Line 2: Format 2: <DD.MM.YY>
questions.constraints: Strict format DD-MM-YYYY (exactly 10 characters), a valid calendar date, year 1000-9999.
hints: Positions are fixed: day is s[0:2], month is s[3:5], year is s[6:10].
Build each output with an f-string from the three slices; no int conversion is needed.
The two-digit year is the slice s[8:10], or y[2:] once you have the year.
questions.reference_solution:
s = input().strip()
d = s[0:2]
m = s[3:5]
y = s[6:10]
print(f"Format 1: {y}/{m}/{d}")
print(f"Format 2: {d}.{m}.{y[2:]}")

questions.title: Fixed-Width Grade Summary
questions.objective: Format student roll and marks into fixed 40-character summary line with space padding.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Format a student result as one fixed-width line of exactly 40 characters.
Given a roll number (integer), a subject code (string) and marks (float), print:
`Roll:{roll:>6}|Sub:{sub:<10}|Marks:{marks:>7.2f}`
- Roll number: right-aligned in 6 characters
- Subject code: left-aligned in 10 characters (padded with trailing spaces)
- Marks: right-aligned in 7 characters with 2 decimal places
The field widths are chosen so the line is always exactly 40 characters.
questions.input_format: A single line containing roll_number subject_code marks (separated by spaces).
questions.output_format:
One line of exactly 40 characters:
Roll:<6 wide>|Sub:<10 wide>|Marks:<7 wide>
hints: Use format specs inside an f-string: :>6 for right-align, :<10 for left-align.
Convert roll to int and marks to float before formatting; the marks spec is :>7.2f.
Count: 5 + 6 + 1 + 4 + 10 + 1 + 6 + 7 = 40 characters for every valid input.

questions.title: Coordinated Time Offset
questions.objective: Apply modular arithmetic on 24-hour clock time to handle forward and backward minute offsets across midnight boundaries.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Given a 24-hour time in HH:MM format and an integer offset in minutes (which may be positive, negative, or zero), calculate the resulting time.
Rules:
- The clock operates on a 24-hour cycle from 00:00 to 23:59 (1440 minutes per day).
- Forward offsets roll past midnight (e.g., 23:45 + 30 mins -> 00:15).
- Negative offsets roll back into the previous day (e.g., 00:15 - 30 mins -> 23:45).
- Output the resulting time formatted with two-digit zero padding: HH:MM.
questions.input_format: A single line containing HH:MM time and an integer offset (separated by space).
hints: Convert the starting time entirely into total minutes from midnight: H * 60 + M.
Add the offset minutes and use Python's modulo operator % 1440 to wrap cleanly across midnight (Python handles negative modulo automatically).
Divide back by 60 for new hours (// 60) and modulo by 60 for new minutes (% 60). Format with :02d.
questions.reference_solution:
time_str, offset_str = input().split()
h, m = map(int, time_str.split(":"))
offset = int(offset_str)
total_mins = (h * 60 + m + offset) % 1440
new_h = total_mins // 60
new_m = total_mins % 60
print(f"New Time: {new_h:02d}:{new_m:02d}")

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing HH:MM time and an integer offset (separated by space).
